items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: The magnetotelluric (MT) method uses natural electromagnetic field variations to image subsurface electrical resistivity at depths ranging from tens of metres to hundreds of kilometres. It is widely used in geophysical exploration for natural resources, including minerals, geothermal energy, and groundwater, as well as in the characterisation of sites for CO$_2$ storage and in studies of crustal and lithospheric structure. The MT inverse problem is, however, inherently non-unique: many distinct resistivity models reproduce the observations equally well. Conventional practice nonetheless reports a single regularised model, with no quantitative measure of its uncertainty. MTGeophysics.jl is a Julia package developed to address this limitation. Its principal aim is the quantification of uncertainty in MT model building, advancing interpretation from a single deterministic model, through an ensemble of plausible models, towards the full posterior distribution. The package also provides tools for data analysis, mesh generation, masking, forward modelling, inversion, model analysis and visualisation for MT research and applications. items.summary: Paper P10 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P10 — Synthesis, physical compatibility and fundamental constants Can the exceptional algebras that organise candidate particle properties also describe the dynamics that selects them? We give a pedagogical research synthesis of nine studies of interacting generalised trace dynamics and its finite matrix extensions. Interactions between spacetime--matter atoms are motivated by bosonic exchange between fermionic currents. An ordered coassociative vertex, its graded selection rules and a positive mediated kernel make this proposal calculable. A selected physical-current model has a common onset of two neutral composite condensates, while separate matrix parents exhibit exact ordering bounds, competing geometric configurations and finite-time record protocols. A trace isometry connects a spin-one matrix sector to exceptional Jordan invariants. For one exact canonical fermion determinant, a positive-squares identity proves that commuting equilateral configurations, rather than the Jordan-bearing balanced branch, are selected sufficiently close to onset. A complementary exact result shows that the polynomial parent's cubic selects associative orientations of the balanced spin-one branch, whose centred Jordan spectrum is a degenerate doublet. Equal spacing is not stationary under those unrestricted orientation variations. Massive canonical fermions can provide positive local orientation curvature, but cancellation of the cubic slope and full vacuum stability are separate conditions. A further fixed-charge parent supports a stable local branch whose Jordan response requires additional collective coordinates. Conserved charges then produce a calculable, coordinate-invariant difference between relaxed static and closed-system slow spectral response. These results put earlier mass-ratio, mixing and gauge-normalisation proposals into contact with explicit vacuum and response calculations. They also identify their remaining inputs: the microscopic physical projection, state, relative family frames, kinetic residues and matching data. Full cohesive emergence of spacetime, matter and classical records, and the measured fundamental constants, have not been derived. The interaction is required to preserve the additive STM sector's conditional spectral framework. Recovery at zero coupling does not establish this compatibility at finite coupling; we formulate the missing projection and backreaction tests explicitly. The achievement is a set of constructive bridges and discriminating tests, with a concrete route from algebraic hypotheses to physical predictions.

An admitted normal–normal–full bound therefore replaces the unrestricted third-derivative coefficient in those terms. The proof retains the full complex normal covector, both inverse denominators, the actual-graph Schur cost, and the separate unrestricted second and fourth derivatives. A noncircular argument uses an already established regular source product to admit the graph and homotopies, and checks the fourth-derivative shoulder separately in the original action domain. items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: This Version 2.1 report places the Maxwell Mass Effect at the forefront of a coherent model for the Venusian atmosphere. The surface temperature is treated as the dependent variable required to support the atmospheric mass against gravity. Solar energy is captured in a shallow topside thermal heating pool, stored as potential energy, and returned to depth by organised descent in the polar vortices under conservation of angular momentum. The sulfuric-acid lifting condensation level (LCL) acts as the thermodynamic anchor (Dew-Point Anchor Hypothesis). A two-component radiative opacity lapse rate then fixes only the geometric separation between that LCL and the infrared emission level. Stochastic inverse modelling with a VIRA equatorial profile, hydrostatic integration and thermodynamic filters recovers a cloud base near 49.6 km, an emission level near 69.4 km at approximately 229 K, and a surface pressure of approximately 91.5 bar. An order-of-magnitude energy-budget test shows that the required polar mass flux lies within the range of observed vortex descent speeds. Version 2 adds a quantitative recirculation (recycle) test using existing Venusian meridional circulation wind data. Observed poleward flows of ~10–15 m s⁻¹ at cloud tops imply a hemispheric Hadley-cell mass flux of order 10¹¹ kg s⁻¹ and a full recirculation timescale of 1–2 weeks. This multi-cycle pathway resolves the apparent single-pass temperature-rise tension and brings the adiabatic signature into agreement with observed polar temperature contrasts of 15–50 K. The same boundary conditions can be satisfied by a conventional greenhouse calculation, but only the Maxwell framework supplies a structural explanation for the polar vortices themselves and a dynamically consistent energy pathway. A new Discussion section explains the changes from Version 1 and how they address independent criticisms of the energy-budget magnitude and the need for a discriminating quantitative test. Diagnostic figures from the inverse model and the recirculation test are included.

items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: This repository provides three physics-based datasets for developing and evaluating surrogate models to identify the seismic failure modes (SFMs) of coastal reinforced concrete bridge bents supported by pile-group foundations under combined scour and corrosion. Each sample contains 20 input variables: 17 structural and geotechnical parameters, scour depth, and the corrosion levels of longitudinal and transverse column reinforcement. The output is one of three SFMs: column flexural failure (CFF), foundation flexural failure (FFF), or column shear-associated failure (CSF). These labels are determined through nonlinear finite element analysis and code-based shear capacity calculations. The datasets support reproducible surrogate model development and subsequent life-cycle probabilistic assessment of SFMs and their transitions in deteriorating coastal bridge bents.

items.summary: Surface code decoders like Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) can also be used to estimate or bound the probability of a logical failure conditioned on the error syndrome commonly called ``soft outputs''. Estimates like the complementary gap of a matching, or others like the ``cluster gap'' are used to produce high fidelity magic states via post-selection. They are also helpful in reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant computation via code concatenation schemes like yoked surface codes. In this work we provide techniques to tightly lower bound the complementary gap of a rotated surface code syndrome block and provide fast parallel algorithms for computing this lower bound efficiently. Our algorithms run in real time for the moderate distances and reasonable physical noise rates required by these applications. We achieve latencies of the order of one to tens of microseconds on sufficiently fast CPU cores.

items.summary: This report was developed within seizmic – Scaling Social Entrepreneurship and Innovation: Zooming in on Multidisciplinary Interconnected Challenges, a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network funded under Horizon Europe. It synthesises insights from four literature reviews conducted within Work Package 3, Impact Investing for Social Entrepreneurship Scaling, to provide a practical framework for understanding how impact investing can support the sustainable scaling of social enterprises. The report explores impact investing as a system of relationships involving investors, social enterprises, beneficiaries, intermediaries, and policymakers. It examines how investment objectives, financial instruments, governance arrangements, impact measurement practices, and ecosystem dynamics shape the ability of social enterprises to scale their social and environmental impact while preserving mission integrity. Drawing on complementary reviews of impact investing strategies, financing instruments, mission drift, governance, and ecosystem coordination, the report analyses how different forms of impact capital support three major scaling pathways: scaling up (systemic and policy change), scaling out (replication and expansion), and scaling deep (changes in values, norms, and community practices). Particular attention is given to the opportunities and challenges associated with instruments such as crowdfunding, venture philanthropy, social impact bonds, blended finance, development finance institution investments, and social venture capital. The report highlights the importance of aligning investor expectations, enterprise missions, governance structures, and impact measurement systems throughout the investment lifecycle. It identifies key risks, including mission drift, coordination failures, reporting burdens, and scaling-related challenges, while proposing practical safeguards and governance mechanisms to foster long-term mission fidelity and impact effectiveness. Based on this synthesis, the report offers actionable recommendations for investors, social enterprises, intermediaries, and policymakers. It argues that successful impact investing depends not only on the availability of capital, but also on the design of investment relationships, ecosystem infrastructure, and measurement practices that remain aligned with social purpose over time. By translating academic evidence into practitioner-oriented guidance, the report contributes to the development of a more effective and resilient European impact investing ecosystem.

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. items.summary: Online sensor telemetry feeds the digital-twin, forecasting, control, and maintenance tools of instrumented water infrastructure. Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. On the held-out final 20% of the record (12 channels in five installations), HARDIO achieves a mean chained 1-NRMSE of 0.976, within 0.0035 of a per-channel oracle, and outperforms the uniform SAITS pipeline (p=0.003). Its reconstruction performance is close to that of the strongest uniform pipelines, without a statistically significant improvement over them, and slightly below that of a single detector-imputer pair selected on validation data (0.978). The released artefact exposes the model map, confidence labels, margins, and production masks for decision support.

items.summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator in the pupil of a microscope objective can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once, but only if the phase pattern it displays is computed well: the pattern fixes how much light reaches the traps, how equal the traps are, where stray light goes, how the pattern survives a real device, and how fast it can be recomputed when traps move. DinHot is an open studio that runs 24 methods (19 published ones and 5 proposed here) on the same task, with the same seeds, metrics and device model, in Python as the reference and in a TypeScript port that runs live in a browser. We describe the optical and device model, the methods with the measured acceptance of each, 14 cases from a 3 x 3 array to a disordered 819-trap array and shaped potentials, the benchmark protocol, two learned models, and the 5 proposed methods, three of which meet their acceptance criteria on their acceptance tasks, each within a scope that the benchmark or the scope measurements narrow (a device-aware weighted Gerchberg-Saxton update, a flicker-bounded phase-continuous sequence and an efficiency-uniformity front), one of which meets a narrowed criterion (an aberration-robust hologram) and one of which is refuted by measurement (a learned warm start for phase-fixed weighted GS). A network trained on three-plane volumes beats its baseline at equal wall-clock on all 162 held-out volumes (median accuracy ratio 1.140), whereas its two-dimensional counterpart ties with Gerchberg-Saxton (ratio 0.9994). The model is a scalar Fourier model of a simulated device, not a calibrated instrument. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: R code, data and computed output accompanying the manuscript “The Unit-Truncated Power Bilal Distribution: Structural Properties, Shape Analysis, and Statistical Inference” by Preut Thanarat, Tharakorn Jaruruataikant and Nipada Papukdee. The deposit is organised in two parts. round1/ holds the five R scripts of the original submission and their output: the theoretical PDF, CDF and hazard-rate figures; the structural summaries, quantile-based shape measures and entropies; the Monte Carlo study over eight parameter configurations and five sample sizes, including observed-information standard errors and empirical Wald coverage; and the FirmCost and SC16 applications with parametric-bootstrap goodness-of-fit calibration, the likelihood-ratio test of the nested unit-truncated Bilal restriction, and the CDF, TTT and Q-Q diagnostics. round2/ holds the revision package as it was run. It adds the expanded comparison of nine named model specifications across four source datasets (FirmCost, SC16, AIS and College) and eight analysis groups, with parametric-bootstrap Cramér–von Mises and Anderson–Darling diagnostics at B = 999 and repeated five-fold cross-validation; the College interval-observation likelihood under an assumed nearest-percentage-point rounding mechanism; the limiting-likelihood and boundary-information analysis; the four source datasets together with the archived cross-validation fold assignments, so the predictive comparisons reproduce exactly; and the computed tables and vector figures. A SHA256 manifest is included for verification, and reference/ preserves the original Monte Carlo and goodness-of-fit sources, including the analytic audit of 6,000 replications. All results were produced in R 4.6.1 using the parallel package with a PSOCK cluster and ggplot2 for the figures; the round-two stages also require the sn package. Random seeds, optimizer settings and the boundary-fit classification rule are documented in README.md. Released under the MIT License.

items.summary: The calibration and test probabilities of every run of a tabular classification benchmark, released so that prediction sets and their metrics can be recomputed without refitting a model. A conformal set is a function of four arrays: the class probabilities and labels on a calibration split, and the same on a test split. This deposit is those arrays, together with the software that reads them. The benchmark comprises 218 classification datasets and 22 models from four families, among them 13 tabular foundation models, each evaluated with the same ten seeds. Of the 218, 178 are real datasets and 40 are a synthetic block generated for this benchmark; three of the real ones are Bayesian-network resamplings of small classical datasets and are much larger than their seeds; of those, only one has its own seed in the collection, so that pair is not independent of itself while a rank test treats datasets as independent. Dataset size does not indicate provenance: the largest datasets in the collection are real. Coverage is not uniform and the per-model dataset count is reported for every cell. Eleven datasets carry more than ten classes, and the in-context models measured on them cannot enter them: one refuses and names the limit, another builds a ten-output head and fails inside a kernel. That is a capability limit observed on the models that were run rather than a property claimed of the family, and it is not missing work. One foundation model is measured on the original datasets only. Anything computed across models should be computed on a complete submatrix: the datasets on which every model being compared has all ten seeds. The calibration rows are held out of fitting, of tuning, of early stopping and of the in-context data, and each cell records which rows they were. The code that does it is included, with the line of each step documented. Probabilities are float64 and are not rounded: a prediction set is a comparison against a threshold, and a point sitting on that threshold moves if the value it is compared to is shortened. The data are released under CC BY 4.0. The software included in the source archive is released under the MIT licence, as stated by the LICENSE file it contains. The datasets themselves are not redistributed: each cell carries the row indices into its source dataset, and the synthetic datasets regenerate from their seeds with an included script. Model weights are not redistributed; every checkpoint is named in the model table. Version 1.2.0 adds the runs completed after version 1.1.0 and changes or removes nothing in it. Three new shards (cells-011 to cells-013, 2.02 GB) hold 311 further cells; index.parquet now lists all 46,182 cells and manifest_1016.parquet is their manifest. The files prefixed blocks_1016__ recompute the two blocks outside the main comparison on the completed runs, with the pipeline that produced the article's tables: the large-dataset block on 49 datasets and 21 models (42 in version 1.1.0) and the many-class block on 11 datasets and 7 models (5 in version 1.1.0). The main block of 113 real datasets and 22 models is unchanged. CHANGELOG.md lists what is added and the pairs that are still missing, with the reason for each.

items.summary: Code and results for the paper "Leakage-Aware, Edge-Deployable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: A Latency, Accuracy and Calibration Benchmark". Motivation: Ashwini et al. (doi:10.1155/acis/2622873) note that most current brain tumor segmentation and classification methods rely on offline, static imaging and therefore do not support real-time monitoring. That paper reports results on the Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI dataset (7,023 scans: pituitary, glioma, meningioma and no tumor). This record addresses part of that gap by measuring per-image CPU latency of four classifiers, as a proxy for real-time capability, and by checking whether duplicate images inflate reported accuracy. Contents: a pipeline that audits the dataset for exact and near-duplicate images, builds naive and leakage-aware splits, fine-tunes MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet50 and Inception-ResNet-v2 over three seeds, measures batch-1 CPU latency, and evaluates calibration. Folders: results (main 24 runs; 7,215 images, duplicate distance 0) and results_laptop (reduced MobileNetV3 runs; 7,200 images, duplicate distance 1). The MRI images are not included; the dataset is on Kaggle (doi:10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/2645886). See README.md for the run order.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: This Python software provides a Docker-based workflow for electroencephalography (EEG) quality control, preprocessing and feature extraction . It supports reproducible research on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents using the task recordings in the BALLADEER dataset. The software documents and implements the processing workflow underlying A task EEG dataset with preprocessed signals and features for ADHD research in children and adolescents . That companion resource contains 669 eligible recordings from 156 participants and 115 feature definitions or templates across seven feature families. The recordings and generated feature tables are distributed separately from this software. What the software does Raw EEG quality assessment: characterizes recording quality before preprocessing and produces structured quality summaries. Recording eligibility and correction plans: applies the supplied, frozen label-blind selection records, including recording eligibility and approved channel-interpolation actions. Conservative EEG preprocessing: processes continuous blocks without bridging acquisition gaps, applies 0.5–40 Hz filtering, harmonizes sampling to 128 Hz, and performs conditional channel interpolation and average referencing. Post-preprocessing quality assessment: calculates quality summaries and comparisons with the original recordings. EEG feature extraction: generates seven feature families using aligned, gap-aware windows of 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds with 50% overlap, subject to each estimator's duration requirements. Output verification: checks processing lineage, cross-stage consistency and recorded checksums. The supplied selection records preserve the decisions used for the companion dataset. Reusing those records does not repeat the original manual review or establish new eligibility decisions for another cohort. Seven EEG feature families Temporal and statistical features. Conventional spectral features. Aperiodic spectral features. Complexity and fractal features. Functional connectivity features. Graph and network features. Time-frequency decomposition features. Feature definitions expand across channels, channel pairs and other indexed positions. Outputs retain calculation states and reasons for unavailable or undefined values. Duration-dependent support is explicit; for example, the configured aperiodic spectral analysis uses 8- and 16-second windows. Supported recordings, inputs and outputs The input is the original BALLADEER dataset, version 2 , obtained from its version-specific Figshare record . Extract the source data before running the software. Set --input-dir to the directory that directly contains users_demographics.json and participant directories such as UB0004/ , preserving the original task subdirectories and filenames. The companion Zenodo derivative dataset is an output resource, not the input to this complete reproduction workflow. The packaged workflow is configured for five BALLADEER task conditions: CogniFit cognitive assessment, Attention Robots, and Slackline levels 1, 6 and 11. Users also provide a writable output directory. The input directory is mounted read-only. Outputs include preprocessed EEG signals in MNE-FIF format, tabular feature outputs, quality summaries, calculation-state records, configuration snapshots, processing manifests and checksums. The software archive includes label-blind selection metadata with pseudonymous recording identifiers; it does not contain the original EEG recordings or the generated derivative dataset. Reproducibility and package contents The archive includes Python source code, scientific configurations, a Dockerfile, version-pinned Python dependencies, shell launchers, validation tests and documentation. Users can run individual processing stages, extract one feature family for one task, or execute the complete sequential workflow. Graph features use the corresponding connectivity outputs. items.summary: CIRCULAR MATERIAL ECONOMIES FOR AUTONOMOUS MOBILE CITIES AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:移動城市循環經濟與材料永續極限 55/90 CIRCULAR MATERIAL ECONOMIES FOR AUTONOMOUS MOBILE CITIES AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy (Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 55 of 90). It investigates whether a deliberately unoccupied six-module mobile-city research system can reduce relocation-related material loss through qualified reuse, automated selective disassembly and auditable remanufacturing, while preserving deployment latency and critical-service safety. The three-way research coupling is Circular Materials x Autonomous Manufacturing x Urban Sustainability. Neither a functioning autonomous city nor a human-occupied habitat is asserted. The falsifiable proposal compares a frozen circular material strategy against competent conventional manual recovery, replacement and stationary emergency infrastructure under equal material, energy, sensing, technician-hour, tool, water and transport budgets. Original intake, declined parts, work in progress, consumed adhesives, repeated repairs, rejected batches and retired material remain in the denominator. Blind faults include grade swaps, hidden fatigue, wrong material passports, replayed scale measurements, contamination, source-energy omissions and optimistic virgin-substitution credits. A proposal fails whenever a load-bearing component, utility service, waste route, safety interlock or material identity cannot be independently reconstructed. Thirty mechanism-distinct research formula plates address mass custody, qualified yield, bond separation work, fatigue, polymer rheology, sensor residuals, covariance, electrical energy, verified lifecycle inventory, carbon-allocation sensitivity, replacement counterfactuals, tail risk, second-site reproduction and noncompensatory physical release. The original contract's cyber-physical residual r_k = y_k - yhat_k(x_k,u_k) is retained as one fault-detection method; it is not treated as a law of circularity or sustainability. Every mathematical plate states units, validity assumptions, a blinded counterexample and scientific chapter interfaces. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 separately paginated research studies and 200 Research Gates, each connected to a specified material state, independent reference, fault or competing process. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose research instruments, material-qualification fixtures, provenance devices, circularity accounting tools and successor-ready evidence protocols. This work proposes hypotheses and reproducibility obligations, not physical trial outcomes. Its complete PDF also contains research limits, negative-result custody and second-laboratory transfer requirements. The scope remains prospective, scaled and non-occupancy. Environmental performance requires functional-unit parity and a complete lifecycle inventory; increasing recovered mass alone does not prove lower environmental burden. Relevant method references include Ostapska et al. (10.1016/j.spc.2024.05.014), Formentini et al. (10.1016/j.jclepro.2025.145459), Attia et al. (10.1016/j.autcon.2024.105521), Mao and Cao (10.1016/j.spc.2024.12.021), Poschmann et al. (10.1002/cite.201900107) and Keating et al. (10.1126/scirobotics.aam8986). The Flagship 13 mother genealogy identifiers (10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839) were provided by the author and their metadata have not been independently confirmed. No external study cited here establishes this integrated F55 architecture.
